raw_case_text:
A 75-year-old woman presented to another hospital with fatigue, right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice, was evolving over several days. She denied fever, sick contacts, recent infectious symptoms, recent travel or new medications. Past medical history was remarkable only for moderate Parkinson's disease. Medications were aspirin, calcium-vitamin D3 and rasagiline. She was afebrile and jaundiced. Haemoglobin was 8.9 g/dL; white blood cells 6.35 k/uL with 63% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes and 13% monocytes; platelets 30 k/uL; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 U/L; alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 104 U/L and total bilirubin 4.5 with 2.4 mg/dL direct fraction. Tests for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis and human immunodeficiency viruses were negative. Autoimmune workup was negative, including anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-Smith antibody and liver-kidney microsomal antibody. Magnetic resonance cholangiogram showed marked hepatomegaly, moderate splenomegaly and nodular areas of decreased T2-weighted signal within the liver and spleen parenchyma. She clinically deteriorated over a few days.
On transfer to Houston Methodist Hospital, she appeared acutely ill and moderately confused. The abdomen was distended, tense and tender in the right upper quadrant; the spleen was palpably enlarged. The white blood cell count remained 6.29 k/uL with 75% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes and 5% monocytes; haemoglobin 7.9g/dL; platelets 9 k/uL; alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, AST 34 U/L and ALT 79 U/L; total bilirubin 16.4 mg/dL; direct bilirubin more than 10 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 123 U/L and prothrombin time 21.2 s, internationalised ratio 1.8, partial thromboplastin time 36, D-dimer 3.41 and fibrinogen 159 mg/dL. Florid encephalopathy rapidly ensued, as AST increased to 1,669, ALT to 518, total bilirubin to 19.8, along with acute renal failure, worsening coagulopathy and severe metabolic acidosis. A haematology consultant noted rare large blast cells on the peripheral smear (3 of 200 cells, Figure 1); peripheral blood flow cytometry did not detect these. The patient expired within few days of initial presentation before planned liver and bone marrow biopsies could be performed.
A limited autopsy of the liver, spleen and bone marrow revealed gross hepatosplenomegaly with diffusely mottled hepatic parenchyma and variably soft and firm red-black nodular spleen. Microscopic examination of the liver and spleen found effacement of the normal architecture by a diffuse neoplastic infiltrate (Figure 2). Residual hepatocytes were necrotic. The neoplastic cells had scant cytoplasm, immature nuclear chromatin and moderate nuclear pleomorphism. Bone marrow (Figure 3) was hypercellular (80%) with expansion by neoplastic cells. While few residual erythroid and megakaryocytic elements were identifiable, there were no maturing myeloid precursors. Immunohistochemical stains confirmed the myeloid lineage of the neoplastic cells (strong positive myeloperoxidase) which also expressed monocytic (lysozyme) and erythroid (E-cadherin) markers. Subclassification of the AML was limited by cellular degeneration, so the process was classified as acute myeloid leukaemia, not otherwise specified.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old woman with moderate Parkinson's disease presented with several days of progressive fatigue, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over several days prior to admission at an outside hospital, the patient developed worsening fatigue, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice without fever. She deteriorated rapidly over the next few days, presenting upon transfer to Houston Methodist Hospital with acute confusion, tense abdominal distension, hepatosplenomegaly, and rapid progression to florid hepatic encephalopathy, acute renal failure, coagulopathy, and severe metabolic acidosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for several days of fatigue, RUQ abdominal pain, jaundice, and subsequent rapid onset of confusion/encephalopathy. Pertinent negatives: no fever, sick contacts, recent infections, travel, or new medications. Home medications: aspirin, calcium-vitamin D3, and rasagiline.

objective.physical_examination: Initial outside hospital exam: afebrile and jaundiced. On transfer to Houston Methodist Hospital: acutely ill, moderately confused (rapidly progressing to florid hepatic encephalopathy), jaundiced, with a distended, tense, tender right upper quadrant abdomen and palpable splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial outside hospital labs: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 6.35 K/uL (63% neutrophils, 21% lymphocytes, 13% monocytes), platelets 30 K/uL, ALP 92 U/L, AST 62 U/L, ALT 104 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL; negative tests for EBV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), viral hepatitis, HIV, ANA, AMA, anti-Smith, and anti-LKM antibodies. Transfer labs: WBC 6.29 K/uL (75% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes), hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, severe thrombocytopenia with platelets 9 K/uL, ALP 92 U/L, AST 34 U/L (rapidly surging to 1,669 U/L), ALT 79 U/L (surging to 518 U/L), total bilirubin 16.4 mg/dL (surging to 19.8 mg/dL with direct bilirubin >10 mg/dL), LDH 123 U/L, PT 21.2 s, INR 1.8, PTT 36 s, D-dimer 3.41, fibrinogen 159 mg/dL, acute renal failure, and severe metabolic acidosis. Peripheral blood smear review identified rare large blast cells (3 of 200 WBCs).
objective.advanced_workup: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed marked hepatomegaly, moderate splenomegaly, and nodular T2-hypointense lesions throughout the hepatic and splenic parenchyma. Peripheral blood flow cytometry failed to detect the rare circulating blasts. Limited postmortem autopsy of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow demonstrated gross hepatosplenomegaly with diffuse architectural effacement of the liver (with hepatocyte necrosis) and spleen by pleomorphic blasts, and an 80% hypercellular bone marrow expanded by neoplastic cells strongly positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO), lysozyme, and E-cadherin on immunohistochemistry.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive postmortem diagnosis of aleukemic/subleukemic acute myeloid leukemia, not otherwise specified (AML-NOS; MPO+, lysozyme+, E-cadherin+) presenting as fulminant hepatic failure, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe thrombocytopenia due to massive leukemic infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow (with viral hepatitis, CMV, EBV, HIV, and autoimmune hepatitis excluded). The patient died within a few days of initial presentation from fulminant hepatic and multiorgan failure before planned antemortem biopsies or chemotherapy could be initiated.
